title: Mishaari Masaggo
author: Chef Amina Hassan
desc: Sorghum porridge cooked in milk and finished at the table with cold buttermilk, sesame oil and a scatter of black pepper — the dish Somali families make for new mothers, the elderly and anyone who needs feeding back to strength.
longDesc: Mishaari can be made from wheat or from sorghum, and the sorghum version is the one that carries the weight of tradition. Made properly it was whole grain soaked and crushed on a grinding stone into a paste; sorghum flour does the same job in ten minutes. The finish is what makes it: sweet porridge, sour buttermilk and a slick of untoasted sesame oil, all in one bowl, and black pepper over the top so it is not merely sweet.
ingredients: 120 ml (1/2 cup) cold water, for slaking the flour
50 g (1/4 cup) granulated sugar, or honey
1 tbsp untoasted sesame oil, or melted butter (optional)
steps: Put the sorghum flour in a bowl, add the cold water and mix until completely smooth with no lumps at all.
Pour the milk and the remaining water into a saucepan over medium heat.
Add the slaked sorghum mixture straight away, while the liquid is still cold, and stir well.
Add the salt and the sugar or honey, and stir continuously as the pan comes up to heat.
Lower the heat and cook for 10 minutes in total, stirring throughout. It is ready when it coats the back of a spoon.
Pour into bowls and add the cold buttermilk to each one.
Add the sesame oil or melted butter, if using, and finish with the ground black pepper.
chefTips: Slake the flour in cold water first and add the mixture before the pan is hot. Flour meeting hot liquid lumps instantly and no amount of whisking undoes it.
Use buttermilk rather than plain milk to finish. The sourness against the sugar is the whole point of the dish.
Milk and water together is the richer version; made with water alone it is lighter and still correct.
Some households soak rice and grind it with the sorghum. Replacing a quarter of the sorghum flour with rice flour gets close to that texture.
commonMistakes: Adding dry flour to a hot pan, which is the one mistake that ruins this porridge outright.
Stopping the stirring — sorghum settles and catches on the base of the pan within a minute.
Cooking it much past 10 minutes, which turns it stiff and pasty instead of pourable.
Serving it without the buttermilk, leaving a flat, sweet porridge and none of the contrast it is made for.
storage: Best eaten at once. Refrigerate up to 2 days; it thickens considerably when cold.
reheating: Reheat gently with extra milk or water, whisking until pourable again. Add the buttermilk only after reheating.
healthBenefits: Sorghum is a whole grain, naturally gluten-free and high in fibre.
Milk and buttermilk together supply protein and calcium.
Easy to digest, which is why it is the dish traditionally given to the unwell and to new mothers.
culturalNote: Mishaari is an essential iftar dish in Ramadan and the food Somali families take to the old, the frail and the sick. It is made for new mothers throughout the afartan bax, the forty days after childbirth, when the household cooks for the mother rather than the other way round.
